text:
**Apollo 13: The Successful Failure**

On the evening of April 11, 1970, a Saturn V rose from Florida carrying three men toward the Moon. Jim Lovell, the commander, was a veteran of four spaceflights and had already circled the Moon once, on Apollo 8. Fred Haise was the lunar module pilot, making his first flight. The command module pilot was Jack Swigert, who had joined the crew only days earlier. The original pilot, Ken Mattingly, had been grounded after exposure to German measles. Swigert trained hard in the final stretch, and the launch went smoothly. By the standards of the time, Apollo 13 looked like routine work. America had landed on the Moon twice already, and public interest was fading. The networks had declined to carry the crew's planned television broadcast.

The ship had two parts. The command module, named Odyssey, was the cramped cone where the crew lived and where they would return to Earth. Attached behind it was the service module, a cylinder holding the engine, the electrical fuel cells, and the tanks of oxygen and hydrogen that fed them. Docked alongside was the lunar module, Aquarius, a fragile, spidery craft meant to carry Lovell and Haise to the surface of the Moon, at a highland site called Fra Mauro.

The flaw that doomed the landing had been built in long before launch. Oxygen tank number two had been damaged on the ground. During testing, it was dropped slightly. Later, during a pre-launch exercise, its heaters ran far longer than intended and stripped the insulation from the wiring inside. No one noticed. The tank passed its checks and flew with a bare spot waiting for a spark.

On April 13, about fifty-six hours into the flight and roughly 200,000 miles from home, Mission Control asked the crew to stir the tank's contents, a routine step to keep the supercold oxygen from stratifying. Swigert threw the switch. Ninety-odd seconds later there was a bang. Lovell, floating in the lunar module tunnel, felt the whole spacecraft shudder. Warning lights lit up, and the main electrical buses sagged. Swigert reported, "Houston, we've had a problem here." Lovell repeated it, a little more formally.

Inside the tank, the exposed wires had arced and ignited the insulation. Pressure rose until the tank burst and blew a panel off the side of the service module. Oxygen tank two was empty within minutes, and tank one began to leak. The fuel cells needed that oxygen to make electricity and water. Without them, Odyssey would soon be a dead shell. Looking out the window, Lovell saw gas streaming into space and told Houston what he was seeing. It was the moment, he said later, when he understood the Moon was gone.

In Houston, flight director Gene Kranz and his controllers had a new job: not landing on the Moon but keeping three men alive. The first decision was to treat the lunar module as a lifeboat. Aquarius had its own batteries, oxygen, and water, meant to sustain two men for two days on the surface. Now it had to sustain three for four. The crew powered down Odyssey to save its remaining battery power for re-entry and crawled into the lander, shutting down nearly everything that wasn't essential.

Next came the route home. The spacecraft was on a path that would swing around the far side of the Moon and, if left alone, return toward Earth. But the service module engine was no longer trustworthy, and the lunar module had never been designed to push the whole stack. Mission planners used the lander's descent engine, the one meant for landing, to adjust the trajectory. A second burn a couple of hours after passing the Moon sped up the return and aimed the ship at the Pacific. Around the far side, the crew passed about 158 miles above the lunar surface and set a record that still stands: the farthest humans have ever been from Earth, nearly 250,000 miles. Lovell later noted dryly that they were not there to sightsee.

Then the hardships of the ship itself set in. Aquarius made so little heat that the cabin temperature fell to around 40 degrees Fahrenheit, and condensation beaded on the walls. Water was rationed to a few ounces a day, and Haise developed a fever and a urinary infection. The crew slept badly, if at all, in the cold.

The worst problem was the air. The lunar module's lithium hydroxide canisters, which scrub exhaled carbon dioxide from the cabin, were sized for two people for a short stay. They were filling up. The command module had plenty of spare canisters, but they were square and the lander's sockets were round. On the ground, engineers assembled a fix from only the materials the crew had on board: plastic bags, cardboard from a flight manual cover, a suit hose, and duct tape. They read the instructions up to the crew, who copied the contraption and fitted it. Carbon dioxide levels dropped. It remains one of the best-known improvisations in the history of spaceflight.

Navigation came next. Without the guidance computer's usual alignment, the crew steered by hand, using the Sun and the terminator of Earth as references. A small course correction had to be burned manually, and its timing was set by the crew's own watches. Meanwhile Mattingly, grounded but not idle, worked in the simulator at the Cape with engineers to write a new procedure for powering the command module back up using as little energy as possible, a sequence never designed or practiced before. It had to work the first time.

On the last day, they went through it. Before re-entry the crew jettisoned the damaged service module and got their first real look at the injury: a whole side panel gone, equipment hanging out. Photographs were taken. Then they said goodbye to Aquarius, which had saved their lives, and let it go. Odyssey's batteries held. The heat shield, which no one could inspect but which had been shielded from the blast, would have to survive.

Re-entry meant a communications blackout while the ionized plasma around the capsule blocked radio. Normally that lasts about three minutes. On April 17, the silence stretched past the expected time. In Houston, controllers watched the clock and said little. After a long minute, Swigert's voice came through. Three parachutes opened over the South Pacific, and Odyssey splashed down within sight of the recovery ship USS Iwo Jima. The mission had lasted nearly six days. The crew had lost weight and Haise was ill, but all three were alive.

A review board led by Edgar Cortright traced the failure to the tank, its damaged wiring, and a series of small decisions, and NASA redesigned the tank and its heating system. Apollo 14 flew the following year and landed at Fra Mauro, the site Apollo 13 had been aiming for.

The flight never reached the Moon, and Lovell never walked on it. Yet people often remember it as the mission that went best because it went so wrong. It was called a successful failure: the engineers, controllers, and crew solved a chain of problems with little time and few tools, and the result was three men coming home.
